generatedProse.concept-context: The School of Sport uses the language of criticality precisely. To analyse a study or a campaign is to separate its claim, its method and its evidence; to evaluate it is to weigh how well the method supports the claim; to synthesise is to draw several sources into a position of your own; to judge is to say, with reasons, what the evidence will bear. Assignment briefs across the school, in sport science, coaching, management and therapy, use these words as instructions, and knowing what each asks is how you give a marker what they want.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two School of Sport students on a sport therapy module write about the same rehabilitation study for a seminar.

Tom writes: the study found that the rehab protocol improved recovery, and the authors concluded it was effective. This is accurate, and it is a description: it reports what the study says but adds nothing of Tom's own.

Amara writes: the study reports faster recovery, but the group was small and drawn from one clinic, so its claim to be effective is not yet secure. This is a judgement: it still reports the study, but it weighs the evidence and reaches a reasoned position.

Both understood the study. Only Amara moved from describing it to judging it, the step the language of criticality names.
generatedProse.summary: The School of Sport's working vocabulary, analysis, evaluation, synthesis and judgement, names the moves of critical thinking. You can now use these words correctly, tell a judgement apart from a description, and name the move a sport brief is asking for. With the mindset, the active habits and the language in place, you are ready to be critical on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's sentence a judgement rather than a description?

items.text: It weighed the evidence (a small, single-clinic sample) and reached a reasoned position.
It reported the study's findings more accurately than Tom's.
It was longer than Tom's sentence.
It quoted the authors' own conclusion.

feedback.correct: That's right. Weighing the evidence and taking a reasoned position is what makes it a judgement.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the sentence did beyond reporting: weighing and taking a position.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's sentence was a judgement because it weighed the sample and reached a reasoned position. Accurate reporting, length or a quotation are all still description.
